source.title: The Spectral Bias of the Deep Image Prior

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how convolutional and fully connected architectures, capacity, and upsampling affect frequency learning and image denoising, extending generalization-related findings to the deep image prior setting. It does not directly measure the natural-label train/test error gap in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper directly measures architecture and capacity effects on frequency convergence and denoising. It does not test random-label memorization or generalization on natural labels as defined by the claim. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures single-image reconstruction, denoising PSNR and frequency-learning trajectories. None measures the held-out classification performance or other outcomes named by V1–V8. In particular, its convolutional versus fully connected comparison does not test V3's image-classification generalization claim. Original generalization findings appear as background.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: frequency bias provides their proposed explanation for DIP denoising, with convolutions and upsampling contributing. Their experiments strongly suggest this explanation rather than establish it universally; Appendix B reports that sufficiently wide convolutional models can learn the higher frequency first.
record.recipe_differences: The study optimizes a convolutional encoder-decoder from fixed white noise to reconstruct clean or noisy signals, and evaluates best-trajectory denoising PSNR and frequency convergence rather than natural-label train/test error.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture (convolutional versus fully connected), convolutional depth and width, upsampling stride, image frequency content, and noise frequency change the reported frequency-learning or denoising behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: Best-trajectory mean denoising PSNR is 27.47 for DIP, 20.54 and 19.17 for fully connected encoder-decoders, and 27.58 for coordinate-based ReLUNet.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In these single-image denoising experiments, frequency-biased DIP and coordinate-based ReLUNet outperform the tested fully connected encoder-decoders.

fits_no_version.finding: DIP-Conv learns the two frequencies at different rates, whereas DIP-Linear learns them together. Greater convolutional depth increases separation; sufficient width can make the higher frequency converge first.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Frequency-learning order in the tested reconstruction networks depends on architecture, depth and width.

fits_no_version.finding: DIP fits low-frequency corruption before high-frequency image details and never produces the clean image in the reported failure cases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: DIP's early-stopping denoising benefit depends on the relative frequency content of image and corruption.

fits_no_version.finding: Trajectory divergence increases with the spatial extent of high-frequency patterns; higher upsampling stride slows spectral-error improvement and produces smoother output at the same iteration.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Image frequency content and upsampling stride affect DIP reconstruction trajectories and smoothing.

record.problems: The denoising comparison uses only 9 images, downsampled by a factor of 4. The paper reports mean PSNR across trajectories and per-image means and standard deviations over 5 runs. Several frequency comparisons are described qualitatively or appear in figures without numerical values. These results concern denoising and frequency convergence, not held-out classification error.
record.rows_left_out: None. All reported quantitative denoising conditions in Appendix C were extracted per image and model; additional figure-only trajectory samples and frequency plots were omitted where they did not provide a distinct numeric or explicit textual outcome.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting alongside natural-label held-out accuracy and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy.
Classification test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
All parts: held-out image-classification error for convolutional versus fully connected networks, local connectivity, learned sparse connections and convolutional initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD held-out performance and dependence on optimizer tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects on held-out classifier error and their dependence on data size, dropout strength and augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap rankings and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Test-accuracy effects of removing memorized examples versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Remove all three V3 verdicts: denoising quality and frequency convergence cannot support or limit the specified classification claim. Table 1's prose calls DIP best despite ReLUNet's slightly higher numerical mean. Per-image values match Table 2. No omitted result in the supplied text tests V1–V8.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label held-out generalization.
Test error as width increases beyond the zero-training-error threshold.

The paper compares architectures on denoising and frequency convergence, not held-out image-classification error; it does not test learned sparse connections or convolutional initialization of fully connected networks.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the training/test gap.
Removing memorized examples and its effect on test accuracy.

rows.subject: DIP
rows.operation_detail: Measured denoising behavior after 20 and 500 iterations on images with added low-frequency noise

conditions.value: barbara.png and baboon.png with low-frequency noise

rows.measure: Whether the model predicts the clean image before fitting noise
rows.value: After 20 iterations, fits noise rather than true high-frequency components; after 500 iterations, fits input perfectly; no point predicts clean image
rows.note: Denoising failure condition, not covered by the listed claim versions.
rows.check: The denoising failure is explicitly reported, but it cannot establish any listed version's effect.

rows.subject: DIP
rows.operation_detail: Compared frequency convergence with increasing convolutional depth
rows.measure: Mean convergence time by frequency component across 10 runs
rows.value: As depth increases, mean convergence time for k2 increases much faster than for k1
rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard deviation measured across 10 runs; numerical values not stated
rows.note: Text reports the directional result; figure values are not transcribed.
rows.check: Depth-dependent frequency convergence does not measure V3.

rows.subject: DIP
rows.operation_detail: Compared frequency convergence with increasing convolutional width
rows.measure: Mean convergence time by frequency component across 10 runs
rows.value: Increasing width speeds convergence for both; k2 convergence time drops faster and is generally earlier than k1 at 1280 channels per layer
rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard deviation measured across 10 runs; numerical values not stated
rows.note: Width changes the frequency ordering and can remove the lower-frequency-first pattern.
rows.check: Width-dependent frequency ordering does not measure classification test error beyond interpolation, so it tests neither V2 nor V3.

rows.subject: DIP-Linear
rows.operation_detail: Compared frequency convergence with increasing fully connected depth and width
rows.measure: Relative convergence timing of two frequency components
rows.baseline: Convolutional models separate frequency convergence times
rows.value: Both components converge at the same time; overall convergence time increases with depth and decreases with width
rows.note: This tests frequency decoupling; it does not directly measure classification test error.
rows.check: Frequency convergence does not measure V3; simultaneous convergence is not a reversal of its classification claim.

rows.subject: DIP
rows.operation_detail: Measured relative trajectory divergence as high-frequency pattern area was increased

conditions.value: triangle.png with controlled amounts of high-frequency pattern

rows.measure: Variation ε between two optimization trajectories
rows.value: Trajectories diverge more when the pattern covers a larger area
rows.note: The paper interprets this as reflecting learning of higher frequencies.
rows.check: Divergence between reconstruction trajectories does not measure classification generalization.

rows.subject: DIP
rows.operation_detail: Compared output power-spectrum error over early optimization at different upsampling strides
rows.note: Figure-only comparison; text says the low-error region grows more slowly with higher stride.
rows.check: Power-spectrum error does not measure V3. Although precise values are unavailable, Section 3.2 explicitly reports slower growth of the low-error region at higher stride.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: DIP has mean PSNR 27.47, the fully connected DIP variants score 20.54 and 19.17, but ReLUNet is comparable at 27.58 (R1–R4); this is denoising performance, not image-classification test error.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: 1D frequency convergence and convolutional width sweep
reader_labels.reason: Convolutional DIP fits k1 before k2 at the stated setting, but increasing width can make k2 converge first at 1280 channels (R5, R47).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: 1D two-frequency signal at the stated convolutional and linear settings
reader_labels.reason: DIP-Conv converges the low-frequency component earlier, while DIP-Linear errors drop at the same rate and it never predicts a low-frequency reconstruction (R5, R6).
